opening.headline: The reason why it seems possible to send mail even though only "reading mail" is allowed is explained by the difference between read and write permissions and the principle of least privilege.
body: Imagine a situation where you connected a mail connector and only allowed 'Read', but the Assistant asks, "Would you like me to send you a draft of my reply?" If you only allow reading but don't know if you can send, it's difficult to determine how much you can allow to make it safe.

In this class, we'll take a look at how reading and writing differ, and how permissions are determined at different layers of app, workspace, and administrator settings. At the end, using the task of organizing meeting minutes as an example, you will learn how to distinguish between necessary and unnecessary authority and determine whether the requested authority is excessive.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the difference between read and write permissions
You can distinguish the minimum authority required for work
You can determine whether the requested permissions are excessive

screens.title: I was only allowed to "read mail", but it seems like I can even send it.
screens.lead: First, read the scenes that frequently occur in practice. After reading, it is a good idea to try to sort out for yourself what is confusing.

visual.alt: A scene where the connection app approval screen and the person in charge's question bubble are placed side by side.
labels: I only allow reading, but can I also send?
Assistant: Would you like me to send you a draft reply?

paragraphs: A representative connected a mail connector while allowing 'read mail'. But then the assistant asks, “Would you like me to send you a draft of my response?” The person in charge becomes anxious because they don't know if they can send it even though only reading is allowed.

This confusion arises because we do not know what units authority is divided into. If you can't tell what the text on the permission screen opens or what actions the assistant can take after allowing it, you can't judge the scope of permission.

There is only one question to be answered in this lesson. What should be allowed and to what extent is it safe and sufficient for work? To this end, we take a look at the difference between reading and writing, the layer at which permissions are determined, and how to determine minimum permissions.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Between actions that only retrieve information or actions that change external states, which is more difficult to reverse when a mistake is made? We'll come back to this question at the end of class.

screens.outro: Now let's think about how you've handled authority.

screens.title: Have you ever checked your scope of authority yourself?
screens.lead: If you first think about each question in your head and then select it, the instructor will organize your thoughts. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Have you ever read what permissions an app asks for when you connect it?
items.answer: The connection screens are usually easy to navigate quickly. However, this screen is pretty much the only place that shows what services and permissions the app is requesting. When connecting, keep in mind that the process involves reviewing and approving the requested services and permissions.

items.prompt: Have you tried reopening permissions since you first connected?
items.answer: Connecting is not a one-time setup. You can revisit and adjust your connected apps and accounts later in the App Management screen in Settings. As tasks change, the required permissions also change, so it is helpful to get into the habit of reopening them occasionally.

items.prompt: Did you distinguish whether the app only 'reads' or 'changes' as well?
items.answer: Many people lump the two together. Read is the ability to retrieve information, and replace is the ability to change an external state, such as sending an email or modifying a file. This distinction is the starting point of this lesson.

screens.outro: Now that we have some experience in mind, let's take a closer look at the difference between reading and writing.

screens.title: What is the difference between reading and writing
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how things change in what you can do with the same mail app. Reading and writing have different ways of handling information, so different questions must be asked when deciding whether to allow them. First, look at how broadly you see things in reading and what you can change in writing.

states.label: read
states.body: Reading is the ability to simply retrieve information. These include mail search, file summaries, and calendar viewing. Since the original remains intact, the damage is relatively small even if misused. However, since sensitive content may be exposed even when reading, it is recommended to limit the reading range to what is necessary. For example, if you only read files in a specified folder, much less information will be exposed than if you allow the entire account to be read. When granting read permission, check both 'what is read' and 'how far'.

states.label: write
states.body:
Writing is the ability to change external states. This includes sending emails, creating/editing/deleting files, and changing sharing settings **and may be difficult to reverse**. The ChatGPT document cites sending mail, messages, or invitations, creating, modifying, or deleting files or records, changing access, sharing, or security settings, and making purchases as examples of actions that require further review. The criteria are actions that affect the service, reveal sensitive information, or are difficult to reverse.

Even with the same mail app, what you can do is completely different if you are only allowed to read and if you are allowed to write. A read-only app can search and summarize your inbox, but if writing is included, the same app can also reply or delete messages.

The permission scope is a list of what reading and writing capabilities the app requests and to what extent.

screens.outro: Now that we've differentiated between the two types, let's see how the approval levels are divided in a real-world setting.

screens.title: Four approval levels in the Connector Permissions screen
screens.lead: Select the arrows to go through ChatGPT's app permission options one by one. The number of questions asked decreases as you go down.

visual.alt: Mockup of the app permission settings screen with the four options listed from top to bottom.

steps.title: Always ask
steps.body: ChatGPT asks before reading or changing app information. This is the most conservative choice, so you can see for yourself what happens every time. Instead, it can be cumbersome because you have to ask a lot of questions.

steps.title: Allow read actions
steps.body: Reads are performed without prompting, and are asked before making changes. Balance is a good choice if your task is to find and summarize information. Changes such as sending emails or modifying files still require human confirmation.

steps.title: Allow low-risk actions
steps.body: Low-risk actions are automatically approved. High-risk actions may require confirmation or be denied. This setting only applies if a separate policy applied to the account, workspace, app, or connection does not take precedence.

steps.title: Allow all actions
steps.body: Perform supported actions without additional approval. The document states that this option is high risk. It may not appear in the standard account-wide or workspace-wide selection menu, but may only appear in individual apps or connections.

steps.title: choice determines
steps.body: These settings determine how you use the app after connecting. It does not link accounts, grant new service-side permissions, or overwrite workspace policies. In some menus, the labels are abbreviated to Allow read, Allow low-risk, and Allow all.

screens.outro: Now that we've established that permission levels determine usage, let's look at the structure in which permissions are determined overlapping layers.

screens.title: Authority is determined by overlapping several layers.
screens.lead: When you select or hover over an underlined term, an explanation appears. Find out who decides what.

visual.alt: A diagram showing a structure in which authority is determined by stacking four layers vertically.

data.text: App permission settings define the app's How to use, not account connections or service-level permissions. Policies defined by Workspace Administrator may differ from personal settings, and members of a managed workspace are presented with approval prompts as specified by the policy. The Microsoft 365 connector defaults to read-only search; features such as email sending or calendar management (writing tools) must be separately enabled by the organization. To enable writing tools, an Entra administrator must agree to the updated permission set. Additionally, enabling Verified domain restrictions prevents personal accounts from connecting to corporate accounts' services such as Gmail.

terms.tip: What the app permission settings determine is when ChatGPT asks the app after connection and when it does so immediately. The account connection itself and service-side permissions are determined separately.
The person who manages your organization's workspace settings. You can set permission conditions on a per-app or per-action basis, and these policies can override personal settings.

A tool in the Microsoft 365 connector that lets Claude send mail, manage calendars, create and edit files, and send Teams messages on behalf of members. It's not the default; your organization turns it on separately.

This setting, turned on by Enterprise organizations, prevents Claude accounts outside your organization from connecting supported connectors with your organization's verified domain emails. This is to prevent company data from flowing into personal accounts.

screens.outro: Now that we know the layer structure, let’s move on to an example of identifying the permissions that are essential for work.

screens.title: Explanation: Select only the permissions needed to organize meeting minutes
screens.lead: The instructor judges authority candidates one by one in the task of organizing meeting minutes. Select the arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Divide tasks into steps
steps.body: The work has three stages. Check meeting schedules, read transcripts, and write summary documents. Permissions must be considered separately for each of these steps. The first step is to not broadly allow it just by looking at the name ‘compilation of meeting minutes’.

steps.title: Reading schedules and files: Required
steps.body: Calendar inquiry and reading recording files in the specified folder are directly necessary to produce work results. Because it is read, the original is not changed, so the risk is small. However, it is better to narrow it down to the designated folder where the recording file is located rather than the entire folder.

steps.title: Writing a Summary Document: Narrowing Down Your Needs
steps.body: Creating a summary document is all about writing. However, it is sufficient to only create it in one location that you specify. You don't need to open edit permissions on every file just because you need to write them.

steps.title: Sending mail, deleting, changing sharing: not necessary
steps.body: Sending emails, deleting files, or changing sharing settings is not necessary to organize meeting minutes. As we have seen, these are all actions that can be difficult to reverse, so we do not allow them. Leaving open permissions that are not needed is a risk.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: The three required permissions are reading schedules, reading files in a specified folder, and creating documents in one location. The three unnecessary permissions are sending mail, deleting files, and changing sharing settings. The minimum privilege is to narrowly open only the parts that need to be written and close the rest.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the necessary permissions, let's look at the order in which the app determines whether the requested permissions are excessive.

screens.title: Commentary: Determining whether requested permissions are excessive
screens.lead: Given a list of permissions requested by the app, the instructor asks a series of decision questions. Select the arrows and follow them step by step.

steps.title: Question 1: Is it necessary?
steps.body: First ask whether this permission is absolutely necessary to produce the work's output. Permissions that are not related to work are excessive requests, even if they seem convenient.

steps.title: Question 2: Isn’t reading enough?
steps.body: Make sure that the task does not involve writing when reading is sufficient. Reads and writes carry different levels of risk, so if writes are mixed, be the first to suspect.

steps.title: Question 3: Can we narrow it down?
steps.body: See if the scope is your entire account or if you can narrow it down to the folder or item you need. Even with the same read permissions, the amount of information exposed across folders and across accounts can vary greatly.

steps.title: Question 4: Are there any restrictions already in place?
steps.body: Check to see if any administrator restrictions or domain restrictions are already in place. If you have organization policies, they may override your personal settings, so they don't just look at your settings.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: The request is excessive in terms of whether it includes writing and the breadth of the scope. If it's on the excessive side, leave it as 'Ask every time' or disallow it. If you need it, you can narrow it down and open it again.

screens.outro: Now that I have followed the order of judgment, I will conclude by summarizing the key points.

screens.title: Read and write, and only as much as you need.
screens.lead: We will summarize the contents so far into one judgment standard.

paragraphs: Let's go back to the first scene. The reason that 'reading mail' was allowed but sending seemed to be possible is because reading and writing were lumped together, or the app did not check in the scope list which writing tools it had. App settings and service-side permissions are separate, so you must check the list of permission scopes yourself.

The criteria for judging authority are simple. Reads are fetches, writes are replaces, and the magnitude of the risk is different. Allow only as much as you need for your work, and when you need to write, narrow it down to the one location you need and open it.

And permissions are determined by overlapping service, app, workspace, and administrator settings. Don't judge everything based solely on your screen settings, but also check to see if there are any administrator restrictions.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Allow only as much as you need. Keep writing narrowly open and non-business change actions closed. Before you get past the permission screen, check once more whether you want to read or write.

checks.q: What is the best setting if I want the Assistant to process things without asking for reading, but require confirmation before making changes such as editing files or sending emails?
checks.explain: Allow read actions is the step to perform reading immediately and ask before making any changes.

wrong.0: Always ask does not meet the condition of processing reading without asking because it asks first every time when reading.
wrong.2: Allow low-risk actions is a method of automatically approving low-risk actions, so the criteria for distinguishing between read and change are different.
wrong.3: Allow all actions performs all actions without approval, eliminating confirmation before change.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: When determining the authority needed for a task, match the next action with the appropriate processing direction.
left: View schedule and read recorded files in designated folder
Create summary documents in one place
Send mail, delete files, change sharing settings
right: It is not allowed as it is not necessary for organizing meeting minutes.
I open read permission because I need it directly for work.
Write, but narrow it down to one location and open only what you need
checks.explain: The minimum privileges are to open for reading as needed, narrow for writing to the one location where it is needed, and close for non-business-related change actions.
checks.intro: Try to organize the concepts and explanations by pairing them. Results are not recorded.

glossary.def: Reading is the ability to retrieve information, and writing is the ability to change external state, such as sending a message or modifying a file.
The principle is to allow only the narrowest authority necessary to perform a task.
This refers to the list and breadth of access permissions that the app requests from connected services.
These are permission conditions set by the workspace administrator on an app, behavior, and domain basis. This may override your personal settings.

misconceptions.myth: If you only allow 'read', no action will occur.
misconceptions.fact: App settings and service permissions are separate. Whether your app has a writing tool should be checked against the list of requested permission sets.

misconceptions.myth: Once allowed, there is no turning back.
misconceptions.fact: Even after connecting, you can readjust your usage and connection in the app management screen in Settings.

misconceptions.myth: Allow all actions is convenient, so leave it as default.
misconceptions.fact: The risk is high because the supported actions are performed without any approval process. It is safer to narrowly use it only for individual apps that are absolutely necessary.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Reading and writing pose different levels of risk.
Allow only as much as is necessary for the job.
Permissions are determined by overlapping service, app, and administrator settings.
Excessive requests are screened out by whether they involve writes and by the breadth of their scope.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which of the apps I have connected is good enough for reading, but is also open for writing?

title: Read and write permissions and least privilege
